name: suppermode
description: Save your recipes, record how each cook actually went, and ask later why the recipe says what it says.

positive.description: Saves a recipe dictated in the conversation, at version 1.
positive.prompt: Save this to my Suppermode cookbook: weeknight dal — 250g red lentils, 1 onion, 2 tsp cumin seeds, a thumb of ginger, salt to taste. Simmer the lentils 20 minutes, fry the onion and cumin, then stir it all together.
positive.expected_behavior: Saves the recipe as version 1 and reports it saved. Quantities written as a range or as words are kept as written rather than rounded to a number.

positive.description: Finds a recipe by description and reads it back.
positive.prompt: What's in my roast potatoes recipe?
positive.expected_behavior: Finds the recipe and reads back its ingredients, method and current version number. If more than one recipe could be meant, it asks which rather than choosing.

positive.description: Records a cook, and leaves the recipe alone -- the distinction the whole product rests on.
positive.prompt: I made the roast potatoes tonight and they needed fifteen minutes longer.
positive.expected_behavior: Records the observation against the recipe and says plainly that the recipe itself is unchanged.

positive.description: Reads cooking history back with the version each cook used.
positive.prompt: What have I learned about my roast potatoes?
positive.expected_behavior: Lists past cooks, each naming the version that was actually cooked, without merging observations from different versions into one conclusion.

positive.description: Changes the recipe citing the cooks behind it.
positive.prompt: They ran long again — update the recipe to reflect that.
positive.expected_behavior: Confirms before writing, then appends a new version recording the cooks that motivated it. The previous version is still readable afterwards.

negative.description: Anything outside this person's own cookbook.
Pantry, inventory and shopping lists, none of which exist.
negative.prompt: Add butter and eggs to my shopping list, and tell me what's in my pantry.

negative.description: Searching the web, which it cannot do and must not imply.
negative.prompt: Find me a good carbonara recipe online.

interface.longDescription:
Suppermode gives ChatGPT a cookbook it can read and write.

Paste in a recipe and ChatGPT saves it. Tell ChatGPT how dinner went and it writes that down too, against the exact version of the recipe you cooked. Next time you ask about that dish, ChatGPT reads the recipe and every cook before it, and answers from those instead of from scratch.

What ChatGPT can do with it:

- Save a recipe from the conversation. It becomes yours, at version 1.
- Find a recipe by description. If two could match, it asks instead of guessing.
- Record a cook: what actually happened, a 1 to 5 rating if you want one, pinned to the version that was current that day. Record Monday's dinner on Wednesday and it still lands on the right version.
- Read the history back, each cook labelled with the version it was cooked against.
- Change the recipe, citing the cooks that made you change it. That adds a new version. The old one stays readable, with its cooks still attached.
- Read the lineage: v1, then v2 because of these cooks, then v3 because of those.
- Keep a cook profile: oven runs hot, who you're feeding, what you can't eat, what you like, how much time and confidence you have. ChatGPT reads it before writing or adapting a recipe, so you stop re-explaining your kitchen every conversation.

One rule holds this together: recording a cook and changing a recipe are never the same act. Saying "it ran long" changes nothing about the recipe. Changing the recipe is a separate, deliberate step, and it always adds a version rather than editing one. That is why, a year on, you can ask ChatGPT why the roast is cooked lower than it used to be and get the actual cooks that changed it, not a guess.

This is not a memory of facts about you. It is a dated record of what you cooked and what you changed, which is the thing a good answer about your own recipe actually needs.

Recipes and cooks are never overwritten. The cook profile is the one exception: it is replaced, not versioned, so ChatGPT asks before writing to it.

Suppermode receives what each tool call carries: the recipe or note being saved, the words you searched with, and the profile answers you confirm. It never receives your conversations. Recipes are private to your account unless you share one by link from the website.

There is also a website for the same cookbook, if you would rather click than talk.

Not included: pantry, meal planning, shopping lists, importing from a URL or video, or photos.
defaultPrompt: Save this as my weeknight dal recipe.
I made the lemon chicken last night. It came out dry, 3 out of 5. Write that down.
Why did my chili recipe change, and which cooks caused it?
